title: "Player impact from lineups"
---

```{python}
#| label: takeaways
from _viz import read, md
v = read("player_impact_validation.csv")
v = v[v.test == "B next-season team net rating"].set_index(["league", "model"])
r2 = lambda lg, m: v.loc[(lg, m), "r2"]
sig = read("step5_final_significance.csv").set_index(["league", "model"])
sr = read("step5_final_series_cv.csv").set_index(["league", "model"])
g = sig.loc[("NBA", "net rating + availability-adjusted strength")]
gw = sig.loc[("WNBA", "net rating + availability-adjusted strength")]
P, L = "prior-season player impact (prior-informed)", "last season team net rating"
md(f"""::: {{.callout-note appearance="simple"}}
## Takeaways
- **Lineups rebuilt for every game since 2003-04 (NBA) and 2009 (WNBA).** In every season they account for at least 95%
  of points and possessions (98-100% in most).
- **Player impact predicts next season better than the team's own results.** Last season's player impact, weighted by
  who actually plays this season, explains {r2('NBA', P):.0%} of next-season NBA team net rating ({r2('WNBA', P):.0%} WNBA),
  against {r2('NBA', L):.0%} ({r2('WNBA', L):.0%} WNBA) for the team's own net rating last season.
- **Net rating plus our variables predicts playoff series better than net rating alone.** Adding availability-adjusted
  strength (this season's player impact, counting only players available for the playoffs) improves NBA series predictions
  ({g.loglik_gain_per_series:+.3f} log-likelihood per series, one-sided p = {g.p_gain_le_0:.2f}); in the WNBA the gain points the
  same way (p = {gw.p_gain_le_0:.2f}). Details on the Championships page.
- **Weighting the archetype mix by player quality did not beat quality alone.** Who is good matters more than which
  role they play.
:::""")
```

## The model we settled on, and why

```{python}
import pandas as pd
ft = read("step5_final_title_cv.csv").set_index(["league", "model"])
fs = read("step5_final_series_cv.csv").set_index(["league", "model"])
fg = read("step5_final_significance.csv").set_index(["league", "model"])
fw = read("step5_final_weights.csv").set_index(["league", "variable"])
names = {"net rating only (reference)": "Net rating alone (baseline)",
         "availability-adjusted strength only": "Availability-adjusted strength alone (ours)",
         "net rating + availability-adjusted strength": "**Net rating + availability-adjusted strength (chosen)**",
         "net + availability-adjusted (offense, defense) + archetype x quality + age": "Net + ours split offense/defense + archetype x quality + age"}
rows = []
for lg in ["NBA", "WNBA"]:
    for m, nm in names.items():
        rows.append({"league": lg, "model": nm,
                     "series called correctly": f"{fs.loc[(lg, m), 'accuracy']:.0%}",
                     "avg chance on eventual champion": f"{ft.loc[(lg, m), 'mean_prob_on_champion']:.0%}",
                     "champion in top 3": f"{ft.loc[(lg, m), 'champion_in_top3']:.0%}",
                     "gain over net rating (p)": "" if m.startswith("net rating only") else f"p = {fg.loc[(lg, m), 'p_gain_le_0']:.2f}"})
md(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False))
g = fg.loc[("NBA", "net rating + availability-adjusted strength")]
md(f"""**Why this one.** *Availability-adjusted strength* is our variable: each team rebuilt from this season's lineup-based
player impact, counting only the players available for the playoffs, so a team that lost its best player late in the
season is rated on the roster it will actually play with. Net rating can't see that.

- **It beats net rating.** In the NBA it calls more playoff series correctly and puts more probability on the eventual
  champion; the gain over net rating alone is statistically reliable (one-sided p = {g.p_gain_le_0:.2f}).
- **In the NBA, our variable carries the most weight.** In the combined NBA model it holds {fw.loc[('NBA', 'avail_now'), 'share_of_total_weight']:.0%}
  of the weight against {fw.loc[('NBA', 'net'), 'share_of_total_weight']:.0%} for net rating ({fw.loc[('WNBA', 'avail_now'), 'share_of_total_weight']:.0%}
  vs {fw.loc[('WNBA', 'net'), 'share_of_total_weight']:.0%} in the WNBA).
- **Why keep net rating in it.** Our variable alone is about as good at calling series but less steady at picking
  champions in some seasons; net rating captures things our lineup estimates miss (team scheme and coaching, and
players with too few minutes to estimate well). Together they are the most accurate and the most stable in both leagues.
- **Why not the bigger model.** Splitting offense and defense and adding archetype x quality and age did not improve
  on the two-variable model in the NBA; with only 13-20 test seasons, extra variables add noise faster than signal.
  In the WNBA it edges ahead on titles but not on series, so the simpler model is the one we use for both leagues.
- **How it is trained.** Season by season, using only earlier seasons, with recent seasons weighted more heavily
  (the weighting is chosen from past seasons only).""")
```

## Other approaches we tested

Everything below led to the chosen model. Roster-only versions use **last season's** player impact so that no
information from the season being predicted leaks in; they show how much roster quality alone can do.

## How it is measured

Every stretch of play with the same ten players on the floor (a *stint*) is one observation. A ridge regression
gives each player an **offense** and a **defense** effect in points per 100 possessions, holding the other
nine players fixed. The ridge penalty pulls small samples toward average, and each season starts from the player's
previous-season estimate. Defense counts as much as offense here, unlike box-score measures.

**Avoiding leakage:** this season's impact, summed across a roster, rebuilds this season's net rating. So
every roster-based prediction below uses **last season's** player impact applied to this season's roster.

## Top players (latest two seasons)

At least 800 minutes. Impact = offense + defense, points per 100 possessions vs an average player.

```{python}
from _viz import read, md, show, LEAGUE
t = read("top_player_impact.csv")
for lg in ["NBA", "WNBA"]:
    for s in sorted(t[t.league == lg].season.unique(), reverse=True):
        d = t[(t.league == lg) & (t.season == s)][["player", "o_impact", "d_impact", "impact", "minutes"]]
        d.columns = ["player", "offense", "defense", "impact", "minutes"]
        md(f"**{lg} {s}**\n\n" + d.to_markdown(index=False))
```

## Does player impact predict next season?

Share of next-season team net rating explained (R²). Each bar uses only information from the season before.

```{python}
import plotly.graph_objects as go
v = read("player_impact_validation.csv")
v = v[v.test == "B next-season team net rating"]
models = {"last season team net rating": "Team's own net rating last season",
          "prior-season player impact (prior-informed)": "Players' impact last season"}
fig = go.Figure()
for lg, col in LEAGUE.items():
    d = v[(v.league == lg) & v.model.isin(models)].set_index("model").reindex(list(models))
    fig.add_bar(x=[models[m] for m in d.index], y=d.r2, name=lg, marker=dict(color=col, line=dict(width=2, color="#fcfcfb")),
                text=[f"{x:.2f}" for x in d.r2], textposition="outside",
                hovertemplate=lg + ": R² %{y:.2f}<extra></extra>")
fig.update_layout(height=360, barmode="group", yaxis=dict(range=[0, 0.62], title="R² (next-season net rating)"),
                  hovermode="closest", legend=dict(y=1.12))
show(fig)
```

## Picking champions (earlier versions)

Forward-chained: each season is predicted from models trained only on earlier seasons. Playoff teams only.

```{python}
c = read("step5_title_impact_cv.csv")
c = c[["league", "model", "mean_prob_on_champion", "champion_ranked_1st", "champion_in_top3"]]
c.columns = ["league", "model", "avg prob. on champion", "champion ranked 1st", "champion in top 3"]
for lg in ["NBA", "WNBA"]:
    md(f"**{lg}**\n\n" + c[c.league == lg].drop(columns="league").round(2).to_markdown(index=False))
```

## Every playoff series (earlier versions)

The same features, predicting the winner of every playoff series, not only the champion.
Log-loss: lower is better; a coin flip scores 0.693.

```{python}
s = read("step5_series_cv.csv")
s = s[["league", "model", "series_tested", "mean_logloss", "accuracy"]]
s.columns = ["league", "model", "series", "log-loss", "accuracy"]
for lg in ["NBA", "WNBA"]:
    md(f"**{lg}**\n\n" + s[s.league == lg].drop(columns="league").round(3).to_markdown(index=False))
```

**Is the gain over net rating real?** Gain in log-likelihood per series compared with net rating alone, with a 95%
interval from resampling whole seasons (above zero = better than net rating).

```{python}
g = read("step5_series_significance.csv")
g["95% interval"] = [f"{lo:+.3f} to {hi:+.3f}" for lo, hi in zip(g.lo95, g.hi95)]
g["gain"] = g.loglik_gain_per_series.map(lambda x: f"{x:+.3f}")
g["chance gain is not real"] = g.p_gain_le_0.map(lambda x: f"{x:.2f}")
for lg in ["NBA", "WNBA"]:
    md(f"**{lg}**\n\n" + g[g.league == lg][["model", "gain", "95% interval", "chance gain is not real"]].to_markdown(index=False))
```

::: {.caveat}
Association, not causation. Plus-minus effects for players who always share the floor are hard to separate, and the
WNBA's 12-15 teams leave wide intervals.
:::
